title: BDLS Pre-Test — Basic Disaster Life Support v3.0
description: Official BDLS v3.0 pre/post-test: 30 questions on all-hazards preparedness, incident management, SALT mass casualty triage, CBRNE, public health, and disaster recovery.

questions.text: What is all-hazards preparedness?
options: Process of identifying at-risk populations for a disaster or public health emergency
Determination if needs are greater than resources
Uniform approach to prepare and respond to hazard regardless of cause
Unique approach to respond to various types of natural disasters
questions.explanation: All-hazards preparedness is a single, uniform framework (command, communication, triage, surge, recovery) that applies whatever the cause: natural, technological, or intentional. Identifying at-risk populations is vulnerability assessment, and 'needs greater than resources' is the definition of a disaster. A plan built only for natural disasters is exactly what the all-hazards approach replaces.
questions.hint: 'All' hazards means the cause does not change the core plan.

questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate authority to contact if an incident of bioterrorism is suspected?
options: Local or state public health department
questions.explanation: Suspected bioterrorism is first a public health event. The local or state health department runs surveillance and epidemiologic investigation, links to the CDC and law enforcement, and starts prophylaxis and containment. A personal physician cannot coordinate a community response, the governor's office acts through public health and emergency management, and alerting the media first risks panic and confused messaging.
questions.hint: Which agency runs disease surveillance and outbreak investigation for the community?

questions.text: What is a blast injury?
options: Injury resulting from an explosive device
questions.explanation: A blast injury is any injury caused by an explosive device. It includes primary injury (the pressure wave on air-filled organs), secondary (flying debris), tertiary (the body thrown by blast wind), and quaternary (burns, crush, toxic exposure). Penetrating debris and blunt blast-wind injury are only single categories, and a 'chemical explosion' describes the event, not the injury.
questions.hint: Pick the broadest definition, the one that covers every mechanism (primary to quaternary).

questions.text: What is one essential component of a regional disaster plan?
options: Consider all types of natural disasters
Rely on FEMA or other federal authorities
questions.explanation: A regional disaster plan must be written, coordinated, and exercised before an event, so roles, resources, and mutual aid are already agreed. It should be all-hazards (not only natural disasters) and built on local self-sufficiency, because federal help often takes 72 hours or more to arrive. Website updates are a minor communication task, not an essential component of the plan.
questions.hint: You cannot write the plan while the disaster is happening.

questions.text: In a scene with hazardous materials, in what zone would decontamination occur?
options: None of these answers are correct
questions.explanation: The warm zone (contamination reduction zone) is where decontamination happens, between the hot zone and the cold zone. The hot zone is the contaminated area where only rescue and life-saving actions take place in full PPE. The cold zone is clean and holds command, triage, and treatment of patients who have already been decontaminated.
questions.hint: Decontamination happens in the zone between the contaminated area and the clean area.

questions.text: How should a responder prepare for deployment to a disaster zone?
options: All of these answers are strategies to prepare for deployment
questions.explanation: Personal preparedness for deployment includes a supply of your own medications, up-to-date immunizations (for example tetanus and hepatitis B), and a health check so you are fit for austere, stressful work. Each listed step is correct, so 'All of these' is the answer. A responder who becomes a casualty adds to the burden instead of reducing it.
questions.hint: Personal readiness has several parts. Are any of these options unnecessary?

questions.text: What is one tool to help diagnose nerve agents?
questions.explanation: DUMBELS (Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia/Bronchorrhea/Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation/Sweating) recalls the muscarinic toxidrome of nerve agents and organophosphates. DISASTER is a framework for organizing a disaster response, SALT is a mass casualty triage method, and ID-MED is a mnemonic for triage categories (Immediate, Delayed, Minimal, Expectant, Dead). None of these diagnose a poisoning.
questions.hint: Choose the mnemonic that lists cholinergic (muscarinic) signs.

questions.text: What is the most common disaster worldwide?
questions.explanation: Flooding is the most common natural disaster worldwide and affects the largest number of people each year, in coastal, river, and flash-flood forms. Hurricanes, tornadoes, and earthquakes can be more deadly in a single event, but they happen less often and in more limited regions.
questions.hint: Think about which hazard affects the most people every year on every continent.

questions.text: Which statement is true about disaster triage?
options: Transport all casualties to nearest hospital quickly
Provide the greatest good for each individual patient
questions.explanation: Triage is dynamic and continuous. Patients are re-triaged at every stage (scene, casualty collection point, transport, hospital) because their condition and the available resources change. Sending everyone to the nearest hospital overwhelms it. Disaster triage aims for the greatest good for the greatest number, not for each individual, and minor injuries are treated last.
questions.hint: A patient's condition can change after the first tag is placed.

questions.text: What is the leading environmental cause of death in the United States?
questions.explanation: Heat-related illness is the leading cause of death from weather and the environment in the United States, ahead of cold, floods, and storms. Elderly people, the chronically ill, outdoor workers, and the socially isolated are at highest risk. Asthma and diabetes are chronic diseases, and wound injuries are a trauma mechanism, not an environmental cause.
questions.hint: Which option is an environmental exposure rather than a disease or an injury mechanism?

questions.text: What is the first step of SALT mass casualty triage?
questions.explanation: SALT starts with a global Sort. Casualties are asked to walk to a set area (assessed last), then to wave or make a purposeful movement (assessed second), and those who remain still and those with obvious life threats are assessed first. The individual Assessment, Lifesaving interventions, and Treatment/Transport come after the Sort.
questions.hint: SALT = Sort, Assess, Lifesaving interventions, Treatment/Transport. What does the S stand for?

questions.text: Which of the following is a function of the public health system during a disaster?
options: Protect population against injury and disease
Transport casualties to local health care centers
None of these answers are functions of the public health system
questions.explanation: Public health protects the population from disease and injury, for example through surveillance, safe water and food, vaccination and prophylaxis, environmental health, and risk communication. Triage, treatment, and transport of casualties are done by EMS and hospitals, not by the public health system.
questions.hint: Public health serves the population, not the individual patient.

questions.text: Which of the following best defines the function of public health?
options: To recognize health threats that may affect communities
To provide emergency care and transport sick and injured to medical facility
To ensure scene safety and security
To prevent, delay, and treat disease, injury, and disability in individual patients
questions.explanation: The main function of public health is to identify and monitor health threats to communities (surveillance and epidemiology) and to act on them at the population level. Emergency care and transport belong to EMS, scene safety belongs to law enforcement and fire, and treating individual patients is clinical medicine.
questions.hint: The focus is the community, and an early warning role.

questions.text: What is one challenge of Incident Management?
questions.explanation: Communication is the most common and most persistent challenge in incident management. Systems that cannot talk to each other, overloaded networks, different terms between agencies, and unclear lines of information all limit coordination. ICS addresses this with common terms and unified command. Recovery, evacuation, and preparedness are phases or activities of disaster management, not the main operational challenge.
questions.hint: After-action reports most often name the same failure in almost every disaster.

questions.text: What is the initial goal of mass casualty triage?
options: Ensure that all patients are treated equally
Remove the dead from the scene
Treat all patients, regardless of injury, as quickly as possible
Sort and assess casualties, identifying life-threatening injuries
questions.explanation: The first goal of mass casualty triage is to sort and assess casualties quickly and to find life-threatening injuries, so that limited resources go to those who will benefit most. Treating everyone equally or as fast as possible ignores the shortage of resources. Removing the dead is not a priority early in triage.
questions.hint: The first job is to find out who needs help immediately.

questions.text: What type of injury is least common after a nuclear or radiological disaster?
questions.explanation: Nuclear and radiological events cause blast injuries, thermal burns, and radiation injury. Communicable disease is the least common, because radiation exposure is not contagious. Infection may appear later as a complication of immune suppression, but it does not spread as an outbreak from the event itself.
questions.hint: Radiation itself is not passed from person to person.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a mental health impact of disaster?
questions.explanation: Fear is a psychological effect of disaster, together with anxiety, grief, acute stress, and later PTSD and depression. Mental health effects often affect more people than physical injuries and last longer. Traumatic amputation and blast injury are physical injuries, and chronic disease is a medical condition.
questions.hint: Choose the psychological effect, not a physical one.

questions.text: What is a nuclear event?
options: Release of radioactive materials to human-populated area
Nuclear detonation and accompanying massive explosion
questions.explanation: A nuclear event is a nuclear detonation with a massive explosion that produces blast, thermal, and radiation effects together. Releasing radioactive material without a nuclear explosion is a radiological event (for example a dirty bomb or a reactor accident). 'A radiation emergency' is the general term that covers both, and 'an explosion' does not specify the nuclear part.
questions.hint: How is a nuclear detonation different from a radiological release, such as a 'dirty bomb'?

questions.text: What is the first priority of all citizens or responders?
options: Be able to help in a crisis
Be ready to immediately deploy to disaster area
questions.explanation: Personal safety comes first for every citizen and responder: protect yourself from danger, then make the scene safe, then help others. A rescuer who is injured or contaminated reduces the resources available and adds another patient. Life support and deployment come only after the scene is safe.
questions.hint: A responder who becomes a casualty cannot help anyone.

questions.text: Which of the following is a clue that a chemical disaster is probable?
options: Known hazard, substance leaking or spilling
All of these answers are clues of a chemical disaster
Multiple 911 calls from the same area
questions.explanation: Clues to a chemical event include a known hazard or a visible leak or spill, unusual odors, clouds or vapours, many 911 calls from one area, and many people with the same symptoms appearing suddenly (for example dead birds or animals). Each option is a valid clue, so 'All of these' is correct. Recognizing these clues early protects responders from entering a contaminated scene.
questions.hint: Every listed clue is a warning sign. Is any of them wrong?

questions.text: Which activity should take place as part of the recovery from a disaster or public health emergency?
questions.explanation: The after-action review takes place in the recovery phase. It looks at what worked, what failed, and how the plan should change, which feeds back into preparedness. Evacuation and SALT triage are response activities. Risk communication runs through every phase and is not specific to recovery.
questions.hint: Recovery includes learning from the event to improve the next response.

questions.text: What does resilience in the PRE-DISASTER Paradigm™ refer to?
options: The ability of the federal government to return things to normal
The ability of a community to prevent disasters
The ability of a community or a person to return to normal after an event
questions.explanation: In the PRE-DISASTER Paradigm, resilience is the ability of a community or a person to recover and return to normal function after an event. It includes physical, psychological, social, and economic recovery. It is not limited to rebuilding structures, does not depend on the federal government, and preventing disasters is mitigation, not resilience.
questions.hint: Resilience means 'bouncing back'. Who has to bounce back?

questions.text: What is a component of a risk analysis?
options: Do the greatest good for the greatest number
Ability to overcome adversity due to a disaster
questions.explanation: Risk analysis (hazard vulnerability analysis) identifies the likely hazards and assesses the community's vulnerabilities to them, so planning and resources can match the most probable and most damaging events. 'The greatest good for the greatest number' is the triage principle, 'needs exceed resources' is the definition of a disaster, and 'ability to overcome adversity' describes resilience.
questions.hint: Risk analysis combines hazards with what could be harmed by them.

questions.text: When does treatment at the disaster scene end?
options: After all casualties transported from scene
questions.explanation: Treatment at the scene continues until every casualty has been transported. Patients waiting for transport are re-triaged and treated while they wait, especially delayed (yellow) and expectant patients when transport is limited. Finishing triage, EMS arriving, or giving the first life-saving interventions does not end scene care.
questions.hint: Care on scene continues as long as patients are still on scene.

questions.text: What sort of treatment may be performed prior to decontamination?
options: Treatment not requiring personal protective equipment
questions.explanation: Only life-saving interventions (for example controlling major bleeding, opening the airway, and antidotes such as auto-injectors) are given before or during decontamination, by responders in the correct PPE. Other care waits until decontamination is complete, so the contaminant does not spread to responders, equipment, and the hospital. Mental health evaluation and other non-urgent care are given after decontamination.
questions.hint: Only care that cannot wait is given before decontamination, and only by responders in proper PPE.

questions.text: What triage category would you assign to a casualty that requires care that can be safely delayed without affecting probability of survival?
questions.explanation: Delayed (yellow) patients need treatment, but it can be safely delayed without lowering their chance of survival. Immediate (red) patients have life threats needing intervention now, minimal (green) patients have minor injuries and can largely care for themselves, and expectant (grey) patients are unlikely to survive with the resources available.
questions.hint: The patient needs care, but a delay will not change the likelihood of survival.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a vulnerable population in a disaster or other public health emergency?
options: All of these answers are examples of a vulnerable population
questions.explanation: Vulnerable populations include children, the elderly, people with disabilities, pregnant women, people with chronic illness or limited English, and people who are homeless or socially isolated. Each listed group depends on others for evacuation, communication, medication, or care, so 'All of these' is correct, and plans must address their needs ahead of time.
questions.hint: Who cannot easily protect, evacuate, or care for themselves?

questions.text: Which of the following is not a way that a chemical may enter the body?
questions.explanation: Chemicals enter the body by inhalation (the most common and fastest route), absorption through skin and mucous membranes, ingestion, and injection. 'Transmigration' is not a route of exposure. It is a distractor.
questions.hint: The real routes are ingestion, inhalation, absorption, and injection. Which word is not one of them?

questions.text: What is a potential illness or injury that would occur weeks after a natural disaster?
questions.explanation: Weeks after a natural disaster, communicable diseases (for example diarrheal illness from contaminated water, respiratory infection in crowded shelters, and vector-borne disease from standing water) become a major threat. Drowning, burns, and dehydration are immediate effects that appear in the first hours to days.
questions.hint: Consider the late effects: crowded shelters and damaged water and sanitation.

questions.text: Which of the following account for most terror events worldwide?
questions.explanation: Explosive devices, including improvised explosive devices (IEDs), cause most terrorist incidents worldwide because they are cheap, easy to make, and require little expertise. Chemical and biological attacks are rare because they are harder to produce, store, and deliver.
questions.hint: Which method is cheapest, easiest to obtain, and used most often?
